title: Making Connections: Logarithmic Scales in the Physical Sciences
overview: The acidity of lemon juice, the loudness of a rock concert, the strength of an earthquake — all are measured on **logarithmic scales**. Because these quantities span many powers of 10, scientists record the exponent instead. In this section you will use the pH, decibel and Richter scales (and a few others) and learn why "one step" on these scales means "ten times as much".
objectives: Explain why logarithmic scales are used for quantities spanning many orders of magnitude.
Calculate pH from hydronium ion concentration and vice versa; classify solutions.
Compare sound levels and intensities with the decibel scale.
Compare earthquake intensities with the Richter scale.
Solve problems with other logarithmic scales such as stellar magnitude and welding shade numbers.
Correct common misinterpretations of logarithmic scales.

lessons.title: Why scientists use logarithmic scales
lessons.body:
Some quantities range over **many orders of magnitude** (powers of 10). Hydronium ion concentrations go from about $10^{-15}$ to $0.1$ mol/L; the quietest sound you can hear is a trillion times less intense than a jet engine. On an ordinary (linear) scale the small values would all be squashed against zero.

A **logarithmic scale** records the *exponent* instead of the number itself:

| Quantity | Linear value | Log of value |
|---|---|---|
| | 0.001 | −3 |
| | 1 | 0 |
| | 1 000 | 3 |
| | 1 000 000 | 6 |

**The key rule of every log scale:** a step of 1 on the scale means a **factor of 10** in the underlying quantity (or a fixed factor set by the formula's coefficient). Equal *differences* on the scale represent equal *ratios* in reality.

> **Analogy:** a log scale is like describing a number by how many digits it has. Going from 3 digits to 4 digits means the number got about 10 times bigger, not 1 bigger.

lessons.title: The pH scale
lessons.body:
$$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$$

where $[\text{H}^+]$ is the hydronium ion concentration in moles per litre (mol/L).

| pH | below 7 | 7 | above 7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classification | acidic | neutral | alkaline (basic) |
| $[\text{H}^+]$ | more than $10^{-7}$ | $10^{-7}$ | less than $10^{-7}$ |

**Why the minus sign?** Concentrations are tiny (e.g. $10^{-4}$), so their logs are negative. The negative sign makes the pH a convenient positive number (4 instead of −4).

**Two directions:**

* concentration → pH: tomato juice $[\text{H}^+] = 0.0001 = 10^{-4}$, so pH $= -(-4) = 4$.
* pH → concentration: rearrange to $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$. Orange juice, pH 3: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3} = 0.001$ mol/L.

**Comparing:** orange juice (pH 3) has $\frac{10^{-3}}{10^{-4}} = 10$ times the hydronium concentration of tomato juice (pH 4). A **decrease of 1 in pH** means **10 times** more acidic; a decrease of 2 means 100 times.

lessons.title: The decibel scale for sound
lessons.body:
Our ears respond to sound intensity logarithmically. The **difference** in sound level between two sounds is

$$\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10\log\left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right)$$

where $\beta$ is the sound level in decibels (dB) and $I$ the intensity in W/m².

| Sound | Level (dB) |
|---|---|
| Rustle of leaves | 10 |
| Whisper | 30 |
| Normal conversation | 60 |
| Normal city traffic | 85 |
| Rock concert speaker | 150 |
| Jet engine | 160 |

**Each increase of 10 dB is a tenfold increase in intensity.** A conversation (60 dB) versus a whisper (30 dB): $30 = 10\log\frac{I_2}{I_1} \Rightarrow \frac{I_2}{I_1} = 10^3 = 1000$ — a thousand times as intense, not twice!

Sound level can also be measured against the threshold of hearing $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m²:

$$\beta = 10\log\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)$$

lessons.title: The Richter scale for earthquakes
lessons.body:
$$M = \log\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)$$

where $I$ is the intensity of the earthquake and $I_0$ the intensity of a standard, low-level earthquake.

* Magnitude → intensity: $M = 2.4 \Rightarrow \frac{I}{I_0} = 10^{2.4} \approx 251$ times a standard quake.
* Intensity → magnitude: 1000 times as intense $\Rightarrow M = \log 1000 = 3$.
* **Comparing two quakes:** $\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = 10^{M_2 - M_1}$. A magnitude-8 quake is $10^{8 - 4} = 10\,000$ times as intense as a magnitude-4 quake — not twice.

lessons.title: Other logarithmic scales: stars and welding glass
lessons.body:
**Stellar magnitude.** The apparent brightness of stars is compared with

$$m_2 - m_1 = 2.5\log\left(\frac{b_1}{b_2}\right)$$

where $m$ is apparent magnitude and $b$ brightness. **Smaller (even negative) magnitudes mean brighter stars.** Sirius ($m = -1.5$) is the brightest star in our night sky. A difference of 5 magnitudes means a brightness ratio of $10^{5/2.5} = 100$. The same formula with *absolute* magnitudes $M$ compares how bright stars would look from a standard distance of 10 parsecs.

**Welding glass.** The shade number of protective eyewear is

$$n = 1 - \frac{7\log T}{3}$$

where $T$ is the fraction of visible light transmitted. Higher shade numbers transmit much less light: a #14 lens transmits $T = 10^{-3(13)/7} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-6}$ of the light.

**General problem-solving steps for any log-scale formula:**
1. Identify which quantity is unknown.
2. Substitute the known values.
3. Isolate the logarithm.
4. Rewrite in exponential form (or evaluate the log with a calculator).

keyTerms.definition: A scale that records the logarithm of a quantity, so each step represents multiplication by a fixed factor (often 10).
A power of 10; values that differ by one order of magnitude differ by a factor of about 10.
$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$; below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.
Unit of sound level; a difference of 10 dB corresponds to a tenfold ratio of intensities.
$M = \log\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)$; each increase of 1 in magnitude is 10 times the intensity.
How bright a star appears from Earth; smaller values mean brighter stars.

workedExamples.title: pH of household substances
workedExamples.problem: (a) Tomato juice has $[\text{H}^+] \approx 0.0001$ mol/L. Find its pH. (b) Orange juice has pH 3. Find $[\text{H}^+]$. (c) How many times as concentrated in hydronium ions is orange juice?
steps: (c) $\frac{0.001}{0.0001} = 10$. A pH difference of 1 means a tenfold difference in concentration.

workedExamples.title: pH with a calculator
workedExamples.problem: Ammonia has $[\text{H}^+] = 3.2 \times 10^{-12}$ mol/L. Find its pH and classify it.

workedExamples.title: Comparing sounds
workedExamples.problem: (a) How many times as intense as a whisper (30 dB) is a conversation (60 dB)? (b) City traffic is 85 dB; a snowmobile is 32 times as intense. Find the snowmobile's level.

workedExamples.title: Earthquake intensity
workedExamples.problem: (a) How many times as intense as a standard earthquake is a magnitude 2.4 earthquake? (b) What is the magnitude of an earthquake 1000 times as intense as standard?

workedExamples.title: Star brightness
workedExamples.problem: Sirius has apparent magnitude −1.5 and Betelgeuse 0.12. How many times as bright does Sirius appear?
steps: Let star 1 be Sirius and star 2 Betelgeuse: $0.12 - (-1.5) = 2.5\log\frac{b_1}{b_2}$.
workedExamples.answer: Sirius appears about 4.4 times as bright as Betelgeuse.

misconceptions.myth: A magnitude 8 earthquake is twice as intense as a magnitude 4 earthquake.
misconceptions.fact: Each step of 1 is a factor of 10: $10^{8-4} = 10\,000$ times as intense.

misconceptions.myth: 60 dB is twice as loud as 30 dB.
misconceptions.fact: 30 dB more is $10^3 = 1000$ times the intensity.

misconceptions.myth: A higher pH means more acidic.
misconceptions.fact: Because of the negative sign, **lower** pH means **more** hydronium ions — more acidic.

misconceptions.myth: A star with magnitude 3 is brighter than one with magnitude 1.
misconceptions.fact: On the stellar scale smaller (even negative) magnitudes are brighter.

misconceptions.myth: A whisper (30 dB) is three times as loud as rustling leaves (10 dB).
misconceptions.fact: The difference is 20 dB, so the intensity ratio is $10^2 = 100$.

realWorld.title: Chemistry and health
realWorld.body: Swimming pools are kept near pH 7.4; a drop to 6.4 makes the water 10 times as acidic, irritating eyes and corroding equipment.

realWorld.title: Hearing protection
realWorld.body: Workplaces require hearing protection above about 85 dB, because each extra 10 dB is ten times the sound energy reaching the ear.

realWorld.title: Earthquakes in Ontario
realWorld.body: Ontario has small earthquakes, e.g. North Bay (2001) at about magnitude 4, which was 10 000 times as intense as a standard low-level quake.

realWorld.title: Astronomy
realWorld.body: Astronomers compare star brightness with magnitudes; the Sun's apparent magnitude is about −26.8 because it appears about $1.3 \times 10^{10}$ times as bright as Sirius.

practice.hint: What sign do the logs of tiny concentrations have?
practice.solution: Concentrations are less than 1, so their logs are negative; the factor $-1$ makes pH values positive and easy to use.

summary: Logarithmic scales compress values spanning many orders of magnitude; each unit step represents a constant ratio.
pH $= -\log[\text{H}^+]$: a decrease of 1 in pH means 10 times the hydronium concentration.
Sound: $\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10\log\frac{I_2}{I_1}$; each 10 dB is a factor of 10 in intensity.
Solve log-scale problems by substituting, isolating the log, and rewriting in exponential form.

questions.text: Determine the pH of a solution with each hydronium ion concentration, and classify each as acidic, neutral or alkaline.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) pH $= -\log({{m1}} \times 10^{-{{e1}} }) \approx {{-log(m1*10^(-e1)):3}}$. Since this is less than 7, the solution is **acidic**.

(b) pH $= -\log({{m2}} \times 10^{-{{e2}} }) \approx {{-log(m2*10^(-e2)):3}}$, which is greater than 7, so the solution is **alkaline**.

(c) pH $= -\log 10^{-7} = 7$: **neutral**.

questions.text: Determine the hydronium ion concentration, in moles per litre, of a solution with each pH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: pH {{p2}} (give your answer in scientific notation)

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many times as great is the hydronium ion concentration in (a) as in (b)?

questions.modelAnswer:
Use $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$.

(a) $10^{-{{p1}} } = {{10^(-p1)}}$ mol/L.

(b) $10^{-{{p2}} } = 10^{ {{ceil(p2) - p2:2}} } \times 10^{ {{-ceil(p2)}} } \approx {{10^(ceil(p2) - p2):3}} \times 10^{ {{-ceil(p2)}} }$ mol/L.

(c) The solution in (a) has $10^{ {{p2 - p1:3}} } \approx {{10^(p2-p1):3}}$ times the hydronium concentration of the solution in (b), because their pH values differ by {{p2 - p1:3}}.

questions.text: The hydronium ion concentration of most chemicals ranges from about $10^{-15}$ mol/L to $0.1$ mol/L.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) On a linear scale from 0 to 0.1, almost every substance (e.g. $10^{-7}$, $10^{-11}$) would be crowded against zero and impossible to tell apart. The logarithm records the exponent, so the whole range becomes a manageable scale from about 1 to 15, with equal spacing for each factor of 10.

(b) The concentrations are less than 1, so their common logarithms are negative (e.g. $\log 10^{-7} = -7$). Multiplying by $-1$ turns these into positive numbers, which are easier to read and communicate.

(c) Chemical A (pH 6) has $10^{8-6} = 100$ times the hydronium ion concentration of chemical B (pH 8): A is weakly acidic, B is weakly alkaline.

rubric.point: Explains why a log scale is used (range of magnitudes)
Correct comparison of the two chemicals

questions.text: Use the decibel scale, $\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10\log\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}\right)$, to answer the following.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many times as intense is a {{b2}} dB sound as a {{b1}} dB sound?

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sound is {{r}} times as intense as a {{b1}} dB sound. What is its sound level?

questions.text: The sound as a subway train passes is about {{r}} times as intense as normal city traffic (85 dB). A worker using a power saw hears a sound level of {{saw}} dB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the sound level of the passing subway train?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many times as intense as city traffic is the power saw?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the risk of each sound.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\beta - 85 = 10\log {{r}} \approx {{10*log(r):4}} \Rightarrow \beta \approx {{85 + 10*log(r):4}}$ dB.

(b) ${{saw}} - 85 = 10\log\frac{I_2}{I_1} \Rightarrow \frac{I_2}{I_1} = 10^{ {{(saw-85)/10}} } \approx {{10^((saw-85)/10):3}}$ times as intense as city traffic.

(c) Both sounds are above 85 dB, the level at which hearing protection is recommended; the power saw is especially dangerous, since every extra 10 dB is ten times the intensity.

rubric.point: (c) sensible safety comment linked to the scale

questions.text: The decibel rating of a sound is $\beta = 10\log\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$, where $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the decibel rating of a rock concert with an intensity of ${{m}} \times 10^{-{{e}} }$ W/m².

parts.label: b
parts.text: A radio turned very low has a rating of {{q}} dB. What is its intensity?

rubric.point: (b) isolates the log and rewrites in exponential form

questions.text: The magnitude of an earthquake is $M = \log\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An earthquake is {{10^k}} times as intense as $I_0$. What is its magnitude?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many times as intense as a standard earthquake is one of magnitude {{m1}}?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many times as intense is the magnitude {{m1}} earthquake as one of magnitude {{m2}}?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $M = \log {{10^k}} = {{k}}$.

(b) ${{m1}} = \log\frac{I}{I_0} \Rightarrow \frac{I}{I_0} = 10^{ {{m1}} } \approx {{10^m1:4}}$ times a standard earthquake.

(c) $\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = 10^{ {{m1}} - {{m2}} } = 10^{ {{m1 - m2:3}} } \approx {{10^(m1-m2):3}}$ times as intense.

rubric.point: (c) subtracts magnitudes and rewrites as a power of 10

questions.text: A "great" earthquake measures about {{big}} on the Richter scale, while a "light" earthquake measures about {{small}}. A newspaper headline claims the great earthquake was "{{big/small:2}} times as strong".
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim is wrong. The Richter scale is logarithmic: each increase of 1 in magnitude represents a **tenfold** increase in intensity.

$$\frac{I_{\text{great}}}{I_{\text{light}}} = 10^{ {{big}} - {{small}} } = 10^{ {{big-small}} } = {{10^(big-small)}}$$

So the great earthquake is {{10^(big-small)}} times as intense, not {{big/small:2}} times. Dividing magnitudes treats the scale as linear, but magnitudes are exponents; the ratio of intensities comes from the *difference* of the exponents.

rubric.point: Explains that each unit is a factor of 10
Explains why dividing magnitudes is invalid

questions.text: The apparent magnitudes of two stars are compared with $m_2 - m_1 = 2.5\log\left(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\right)$, where $b$ is brightness. Star A has apparent magnitude {{ma}} and star B has apparent magnitude {{mb}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which star appears brighter? Explain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many times as bright does the brighter star appear?

parts.label: c
parts.text: What brightness ratio corresponds to a difference of exactly 5 magnitudes?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Star A has the smaller magnitude, so it appears brighter.

(b) Let star 1 = A, star 2 = B: ${{mb}} - ({{ma}}) = 2.5\log\frac{b_A}{b_B}$

$\log\frac{b_A}{b_B} = \frac{ {{mb - ma:3}} }{2.5} = {{(mb-ma)/2.5:4}} \Rightarrow \frac{b_A}{b_B} = 10^{ {{(mb-ma)/2.5:4}} } \approx {{10^((mb-ma)/2.5):3}}$.

(c) A difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to $10^{5/2.5} = 100$ times the brightness.

rubric.point: Identifies the brighter star with reason

questions.text: Welders use a logarithmic scale to choose protective eyewear. The shade number, $n$, is $n = 1 - \dfrac{7\log T}{3}$, where $T$ is the fraction of visible light the glass transmits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What shade number transmits $10^{-{{k}} }$ of the light?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What fraction of light does #{{s}} welding glass transmit?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many times as much visible light is transmitted by #2 glasses as by #{{s}} glasses?

rubric.point: (b) isolates log T and rewrites in exponential form

questions.text: A student says: "According to the decibel scale, a whisper (30 dB) is three times as loud as the rustle of leaves (10 dB)." Correct the statement and justify your correction.
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement is false. The difference is $30 - 10 = 20$ dB, so

$$20 = 10\log\frac{I_2}{I_1} \Rightarrow \frac{I_2}{I_1} = 10^2 = 100$$

A whisper is **100 times as intense** as rustling leaves. The decibel scale is logarithmic: each 10 dB increase is a tenfold increase in intensity, so you cannot compare decibel values by dividing them.

rubric.point: Explains the logarithmic nature of the scale

questions.text: The pH of vinegar ranges between {{lo}} and {{hi}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the range of hydronium ion concentration in vinegar. Give the largest value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify vinegar as acidic, neutral or alkaline.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many times as concentrated is the strongest vinegar as the weakest?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$. At pH {{lo}}: $10^{-{{lo}} } \approx {{10^(-lo):3}}$ mol/L. At pH {{hi}}: $10^{-{{hi}} } \approx {{10^(-hi):3}}$ mol/L.

So $[\text{H}^+]$ ranges from about ${{10^(-hi):3}}$ to ${{10^(-lo):3}}$ mol/L. (Lower pH ↔ higher concentration.)

(b) Vinegar is acidic, because its pH is below 7.

(c) The strongest vinegar has $10^{ {{hi - lo:2}} } \approx {{10^(hi-lo):3}}$ times the hydronium ion concentration of the weakest.

rubric.point: Correct concentration at the lower pH
Correct concentration at the higher pH
Range stated in the correct order

questions.text: Astronauts record the absolute magnitudes of three unknown stars: Cheryl-XI (0.4), Roccolus-III (−1.8) and Biffidus-V (3.2). Absolute magnitudes compare true brightness using $M_2 - M_1 = 2.5\log\left(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\right)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many times as bright, in absolute terms, is the brightest star as the least bright star?

parts.label: b
parts.text: If the stars have the same apparent brightness, rank them by distance from the astronaut. Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Roccolus-III has the smallest absolute magnitude, so it is the brightest.

(i) Compared with Cheryl-XI: $0.4 - (-1.8) = 2.2 = 2.5\log\frac{b_1}{b_2} \Rightarrow \frac{b_1}{b_2} = 10^{0.88} \approx 7.6$.

(ii) Compared with Biffidus-V: $3.2 - (-1.8) = 5.0 = 2.5\log\frac{b_1}{b_2} \Rightarrow \frac{b_1}{b_2} = 10^{2} = 100$.

(b) If the three stars *appear* equally bright, the one that is truly brightest must be farthest away. Ranked from farthest to nearest: Roccolus-III, Cheryl-XI, Biffidus-V.

rubric.point: Correct ratio for the second brightest
Correct ratio for the least bright
Correct ranking by distance with reasoning

questions.text: Describe the common features of the pH, decibel and Richter scales, and explain why logarithmic scales are useful in the physical sciences.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Common features:**
* Each records a **logarithm** of a quantity (concentration, intensity) rather than the quantity itself.
* Each unit step on the scale represents a constant **ratio** (×10 for pH and Richter, ×10 per 10 dB for sound).
* Comparisons are made by **subtracting** scale values and rewriting as a power of 10.
* pH has a negative sign so that values are positive; decibels have a factor of 10 so values are convenient whole numbers.

**Why useful:** the quantities measured vary over many orders of magnitude (e.g. $10^{-15}$ to $10^{-1}$ mol/L, or a trillion-fold range of sound intensity). A log scale compresses this range into small, easy-to-compare numbers and matches how humans perceive some quantities (hearing, brightness).

rubric.point: Identifies that each scale uses a logarithm of the quantity
Explains each step represents a constant ratio
Explains the usefulness for large ranges

questions.text: Earthquakes in Ontario: an earthquake in Welland measured {{w}} on the Richter scale; one in St. Catharines measured {{s}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many times as intense as a standard earthquake was the Welland earthquake?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many times as intense was the Welland earthquake as the St. Catharines earthquake?

parts.label: c
parts.text: The most intense earthquakes measured are about 8.9. Compare them with a standard earthquake.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\frac{I}{I_0} = 10^{ {{w}} } \approx {{10^w:3}}$ times a standard low-level earthquake.

(b) $\dfrac{I_W}{I_S} = 10^{ {{w}} - {{s}} } = 10^{ {{w - s:2}} } \approx {{10^(w-s):3}}$ times as intense.

(c) An earthquake of magnitude 8.9 is $10^{8.9} \approx 7.9 \times 10^8$ times as intense as a standard earthquake — about $10^{ {{8.9 - w:2}} }$ times the Welland earthquake.

rubric.point: (b) correct ratio from the difference of magnitudes

questions.text: Ammonia has a hydronium ion concentration of ${{m}} \times 10^{-12}$ mol/L.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the pH of ammonia?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify ammonia as acidic, neutral or alkaline.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many times as great is the hydronium ion concentration of pure water?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) pH $= -\log({{m}} \times 10^{-12}) \approx {{-log(m*10^(-12)):4}}$.

(b) Ammonia is alkaline, because its pH is greater than 7.

(c) Pure water (pH 7) has $10^{-7}$ mol/L, which is about $\dfrac{10^{-7}}{ {{m}} \times 10^{-12} } \approx {{10^(-7)/(m*10^(-12)):3}}$ times the hydronium concentration of ammonia.
